## High school academics

Turning to high school academic accomplishments — ACT/AP/PSEO participation, ACT composite score, the three MCA subject scores, CTE achievement level, and CTE course intensity — this block produces the two strongest bivariate relationships found anywhere in this disconnection analysis so far, alongside several null or near-null results.

**Total CTE courses taken** shows by far the strongest and cleanest relationship of any variable examined in this entire bivariate phase (F = 114.407, p \< .001; sumsq for disconnected.cat is 5,039.9 versus 193,432.1 for residuals, roughly 2.5% of variance explained — modest in absolute terms, but an order of magnitude larger than any other continuous predictor examined here). The relationship is a **fully monotonic dose-response**, and every single pairwise Tukey comparison across all four categories is statistically significant: consistently attached individuals take the most CTE courses, followed by intermittently disconnected, then broadly disconnected, then persistently disconnected individuals take the fewest (persistently disconnected vs. consistently attached: −1.52 courses, p \< .001; persistently vs. intermittently: −1.17 courses, p \< .001; persistently vs. broadly: −0.81 courses, p \< .001). This is the clearest, most complete gradient found anywhere in the bivariate work to date — every category is meaningfully and significantly distinct from every other category, not just the extremes.

**CTE achievement level** (the categorical measure) shows the strongest categorical association found in this bivariate phase (Cramer's V = 0.106, p \< .001) — more than double the next-strongest categorical variable examined. The pattern is sharply protective: persistent disconnection is 44.8% among CTE Concentrators/Completors, 49.9% among CTE Participants, and 63.3% among those with no CTE participation at all — an 18.5-percentage-point gap between the highest and lowest CTE engagement levels. Consistently attached rates follow the same clean gradient in reverse (16.6% for Concentrators/Completors, 13.7% for Participants, 8.6% for No CTE). Together with the course-intensity finding above, CTE engagement — in both its categorical and continuous forms — is unambiguously the single strongest predictor of disconnection persistence identified in this entire bivariate analysis, consistent with CTE's role as the most reliable positive lever found throughout every other part of this project.

**Having taken the ACT** shows a real, protective association (Cramer's V = 0.075, p \< .001) — smaller than CTE but comparable in magnitude to the strongest demographic and high-school-characteristic associations found earlier. ACT-takers show a lower persistent disconnection rate (46.2%) than non-takers (53.4%), and a higher consistently attached rate (15.9% vs. 12.6%). This mirrors the "engagement is protective" pattern found for ACT-taking throughout the workforce-attachment models earlier in this project.

**PSEO participation** shows a weak but significant protective association (Cramer's V = 0.038, p = .005). PSEO participants show a lower persistent disconnection rate (47.3%) than non-participants (51.2%), and a modestly higher consistently attached rate (16.8% vs. 14.0%).

**ACT composite score** (among ACT-takers only, N = 5,482) shows a significant association (F = 12.637, p \< .001), but — notably — in the **opposite direction** from CTE and ACT participation: **persistently disconnected individuals who took the ACT scored significantly *higher*, on average, than both consistently attached (+0.681, p \< .001) and intermittently disconnected test-takers (+0.818, p \< .001)**. Broadly disconnected test-takers also scored significantly higher than intermittently disconnected ones (+0.561, p = .035). This is a genuinely important and somewhat counterintuitive finding worth flagging explicitly: among non-completers who took the ACT, higher achievement is associated with *worse* long-run workforce attachment, not better — directly consistent with the achievement-versus-regional-retention tension found throughout the completer-inclusive workforce models earlier in this project (higher ACT scores predicting leaving the region), now appearing again here in a genuinely different outcome (persistent disconnection rather than regional attachment specifically). This is worth foregrounding in the eventual narrative, since it cuts against the intuitive assumption that higher academic achievement should be protective against disconnection.

**MCA Math** shows a significant, and here **cleanly monotonic in the expected direction**, association (F = 17.080, p \< .001): consistently attached individuals have the highest average MCA Math scores, declining step-wise through intermittently disconnected (−0.139 vs. consistent, p \< .001), broadly disconnected (−0.190, p \< .001), to persistently disconnected (−0.202 vs. consistent, p \< .001; and −0.063 lower than intermittently disconnected, p = .040). This is worth flagging as a genuine divergence from the ACT-score finding directly above: MCA Math points in the *protective* direction (higher score, less disconnection) while ACT composite score points in the *risk* direction (higher score, more disconnection) — the two academic-achievement measures tell opposite stories here, which is a meaningful inconsistency worth investigating further before drawing conclusions about "academic achievement" as a single construct in this context. It's also a reminder of the earlier documented concern about MCA Math's substantial English-learner-linked missingness, which should temper how confidently this particular contrast is read.

**MCA Reading** shows a weaker, partial association (F = 5.524, p = .001): only the persistently disconnected vs. consistently attached comparison reaches significance (−0.104, p = .001), with all other pairwise comparisons non-significant, including the persistently vs. intermittently disconnected comparison, which falls just short (p = .054). This is a real but much less clean finding than MCA Math.

**MCA Science shows no significant relationship** with disconnection persistence (F = 1.980, p = .115) — a genuine null result.

**AP exam participation shows no significant relationship** with disconnection persistence (Cramer's V = 0.012, p = .584) — also a genuine null, and a notable departure from AP exam participation's consistently negative association with regional attachment found throughout the completer-inclusive workforce models and the year-5 Part 2 non-completer sequence. Among non-completers specifically, whether someone took an AP exam at all appears unrelated to their disconnection trajectory (worth noting the small subgroup size here — only 869 of 13,177 took an AP exam — which limits statistical power for this comparison).

[**Summary of high school academic accomplishments**]{.underline}

This block produces the two strongest bivariate findings in the entire disconnection analysis: CTE course intensity (the cleanest, fully monotonic dose-response found anywhere) and CTE achievement level (the strongest categorical effect size found anywhere), both confirming CTE as the single most reliable protective factor against disconnection, consistent with its role throughout every other part of this project. ACT-taking and PSEO participation both show modest protective associations, continuing the "engagement is protective" pattern found elsewhere. The most substantively interesting finding, however, is the divergence between ACT composite score (higher score, *more* persistent disconnection — consistent with the achievement-versus-retention tension found in the workforce models) and MCA Math (higher score, *less* persistent disconnection) — two academic-achievement measures pointing in opposite directions for the same outcome, which deserves explicit attention in the eventual write-up rather than being smoothed over as "academic achievement matters." MCA Reading shows a weaker, partial version of the MCA Math pattern; MCA Science and AP exam participation show no relationship at all. Overall, this block shows considerably stronger and more informative associations than either the demographic or high-school-characteristic blocks examined earlier, suggesting that high school accomplishments — CTE in particular — are the more promising lever for understanding and addressing disconnection persistence than demographic background or community context.

## Post-secondary

Turning to postsecondary attendance without completion (`attended.ps`), this is the final variable in the bivariate sequence and it produces the **strongest association of any variable examined in this entire disconnection analysis** (Cramer's V = 0.132, p \< .001) — larger than CTE achievement level (0.106), gender (0.109), or any other demographic, high-school-characteristic, or academic-accomplishment variable examined so far.

**Having attended some postsecondary education, even without completing it, is strongly protective against persistent disconnection.** Individuals who attended some postsecondary education show a persistent disconnection rate of 42.8%, compared to 54.9% for those who never attended — a 12.1-percentage-point gap, the largest raw gap of any variable examined in this bivariate phase. The protective pattern holds cleanly across the milder categories too: attendees show a notably higher consistently attached rate (18.3% vs. 11.4%) and a higher intermittently disconnected rate (27.6% vs. 22.4%), while the broadly disconnected rate is essentially identical between the two groups (11.3% vs. 11.3%) — meaning the entire gap is concentrated in the shift from persistent disconnection toward consistent or intermittent attachment, not in the middle category.

**This is directly consistent with, and substantially reinforces, the `attended.ps` finding from the earlier year 1/5/10 multivariate non-completer sequence.** There, having attempted but not completed postsecondary education showed a large, significant positive association with workforce attachment at year 1 under both outcome specifications (region-or-MN: OR = 2.24; region-only: OR = 2.08) before fading to non-significance by year 10. This bivariate finding — using the full five-year disconnection trajectory rather than a single-year snapshot — confirms that the "tried college" signal is not just a short-term boost visible at year 1, but is associated with a meaningfully better five-year disconnection trajectory overall. Given that the multivariate work showed this effect concentrated early and fading by year 10, it's worth keeping in mind that this bivariate five-year measure is likely picking up primarily the early-career portion of that benefit, since years 1–5 is exactly the window where the multivariate `attended.ps` effect was still significant (or only beginning to fade) under both specifications.

[**Summary**]{.underline}

`attended.ps` is the single strongest bivariate predictor of disconnection persistence identified in this entire analysis, surpassing even CTE achievement and course intensity in standardized effect size. Combined with the CTE findings from the prior block, the picture that emerges is that the two strongest levers against persistent disconnection among non-college graduates are (1) engaging with CTE coursework in high school, and (2) attempting postsecondary education even without completing it — both forms of continued engagement with structured education or training, as opposed to demographic background or local context, which showed comparatively weak associations throughout this analysis. This reinforces the conclusion reached after the demographic and high-school-characteristic blocks: persistent disconnection is best explained by what happens during and after high school in terms of engagement and preparation, not by who a person is or where they're from.

## Summary: Bivariate Predictors of Overall Disconnection Persistence (`disconnected.cat`)

| Rank | Variable | Block | Statistic | Significant? |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | Total CTE courses taken | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 13,173) = 114.407, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 2 | Attended postsecondary (attended.ps) | Postsecondary | Cramér's V = 0.132, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 3 | CTE achievement status | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.106, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 4 | Gender | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.109, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 5 | MCA Math | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 11,869) = 17.080, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 6 | Average county unemployment rate | HS Characteristics | F(3, 13,173) = 16.259, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 7 | Special education status | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.075, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 8 | ACT participation (took.ACT) | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.075, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 9 | ACT composite score | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 5,482) = 12.637, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 10 | English learner status | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.067, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 11 | Non-English home language | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.066, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 12 | Economic Development Region (EDR) | HS Characteristics | Cramér's V = 0.053, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 13 | Race/Ethnicity | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.053, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 14 | Economic status | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.047, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 15 | MCA Reading | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 11,698) = 5.524, p = .001 | Yes (partial) |
| 16 | PSEO participation | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.038, p = .005 | Yes |
| 17 | District rurality (Dem_Desc) | HS Characteristics | Cramér's V = 0.025, p = .010 | Yes (weak) |
| 18 | AP exam participation | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.012, p = .584 | **No** |
| 19 | MCA Science | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 9,147) = 1.980, p = .115 | **No** |
| 20 | Average county wages (% of state avg.) | HS Characteristics | F(3, 13,173) = 1.276, p = .281 | **No** |

Across all four blocks of independent variables examined — demographics, high school characteristics, high school accomplishments, and the single available postsecondary variable — there are statistically significant relationships with disconnection persistence category among non-college graduates in Southwest Minnesota, though three variables (AP exam participation, MCA Science, and average county wages) show no significant relationship at all. As with every dependent variable examined earlier in this project, the associations found here are weak in absolute effect-size terms — none reach even the "modest" threshold typically applied to Cramér's V or η² — but the *pattern* of which variables matter most, and in some cases the *direction* those relationships run, is distinctly different from the postsecondary completion and workforce-attachment outcomes examined earlier.

**High school characteristics show only weak associations, comparable to or weaker than the demographic block.** Average county unemployment rate is significant but non-monotonic rather than linear: intermittently and broadly disconnected individuals come from areas with higher local unemployment than either consistently attached or persistently disconnected individuals, who are statistically indistinguishable from one another — a pattern suggesting local labor market conditions distinguish occasional from no disconnection, but say little about who becomes chronically disconnected. EDR shows a modest association, consistent with the EDR 6E advantage found throughout the earlier non-completer multivariate work. District rurality (Dem_Desc) is the weakest significant finding in the entire table, and average county wages shows no relationship whatsoever — a genuine departure from local wages' consistently strong role in the workforce-attachment models earlier in this project.

**High school accomplishments contain the two strongest findings in this entire analysis, and reveal a genuinely important internal inconsistency worth flagging explicitly.** Total CTE courses taken shows by far the strongest, cleanest relationship found anywhere in this bivariate work — a fully monotonic, dose-response gradient in which every pairwise comparison across all four disconnection categories is significant. CTE achievement status shows a similarly strong, consistent categorical pattern. ACT participation and PSEO participation are both significantly protective, in line with the "engagement helps" pattern found throughout the rest of this project. ACT composite score is also significant, but here it runs in the *risk* direction — among ACT-takers, higher scores are associated with a *greater* likelihood of persistent disconnection, directly consistent with the achievement-versus-regional-retention tension found throughout the completer-inclusive workforce models earlier in this project. This stands in direct tension with MCA Math, which is significant in the opposite (protective) direction — higher MCA Math scores associate with *less* persistent disconnection, in a clean monotonic pattern. Having two academic-achievement measures point in opposite directions for the same outcome is a substantive finding in its own right and should be named explicitly in any write-up rather than smoothed into a single "achievement matters" narrative. MCA Reading shows a weaker, partial version of the MCA Math pattern, while MCA Science and AP exam participation show no relationship at all.

**Demographic characteristics show only weak-to-modest associations, consistent with the pattern found for postsecondary and workforce outcomes examined earlier — though the specific variables and directions that matter here differ from those outcomes.** Gender shows the strongest demographic association, with women more likely to be persistently disconnected than men — a notable reversal from the postsecondary models earlier in this project, where women consistently showed better outcomes. Special education status, English learner status, and non-English home language all show real, if modest, associations pointing toward greater disconnection risk for these groups. Race/ethnicity is weaker in standardized effect size but reveals a substantively important pattern: American Indian graduates show by far the highest rate of persistent disconnection and the lowest rate of consistent attachment of any racial/ethnic group, consistent with the American Indian disparities found throughout this project's other outcomes. Economic status — one of the strongest predictors of postsecondary outcomes throughout this entire project — shows almost no relationship with disconnection persistence here.

**The single postsecondary variable available for this population — attended.ps — shows the single strongest categorical association found for this dependent variable (Cramér's V = 0.132).** Individuals who attended some postsecondary education without completing show a meaningfully lower rate of persistent disconnection (42.8%) than those who never attended (54.9%), the largest raw percentage-point gap of any variable examined, suggesting that even unsuccessful postsecondary attempts carry a substantial protective association with later workforce connection.

**Overall Conclusion**

Taken together, these findings indicate that disconnection persistence among non-college graduates in Southwest Minnesota is driven by a genuinely different mix of factors than the postsecondary completion and workforce-attachment outcomes examined earlier in this project. High school context — district rurality, EDR, local wages — contributes only weakly here, in contrast to its stronger role elsewhere. What stands out instead is high school accomplishment, and CTE engagement specifically: total CTE courses taken and CTE achievement status are the two strongest predictors found anywhere in this bivariate analysis, reinforcing CTE's role throughout this entire project as the single most reliable protective factor for non-completers. Attempting postsecondary education, even without finishing, shows the strongest categorical relationship of any variable examined and directly corroborates the year 1/5/10 multivariate finding that this "tried college" signal is protective, at least in the early-to-mid career years this five-year measure captures. The demographic disparities that dominated the postsecondary completion and credential-level models earlier in this project — especially economic status and special education status — are comparatively muted here, with the notable exception of the American Indian disparity, which remains large and consistent with the rest of this project. The clearest tension worth carrying forward into the write-up is the split between ACT composite score (higher score, more disconnection) and MCA Math (higher score, less disconnection) — two measures of academic achievement pointing in opposite directions for the same outcome, a genuine nuance that deserves its own explanation rather than a single blanket statement about "achievement" and disconnection risk. Overall, the policy implication is that CTE access and continued postsecondary engagement — not demographic-targeted interventions — appear to be the more actionable levers for addressing persistent disconnection specifically among non-college graduates in this region.

# Relationship Between Individual Characteristics and Non-sustaining Categories

The next sections focus on exploring what relationships exist between individual characteristics and the frequency of having non-sustained workforce participation in the first 5 years after formal education.

- **Never non-sustained** — 0 of the first 5 years (post-high-school or post-postsecondary-exit) were classified as "Non-sustained WF"
- **Intermittently non-sustained** — 1-2 of the first 5 years were "Non-sustained WF"
- **Broadly non-sustained** — exactly 3 of the first 5 years were "Non-sustained WF"
- **Persistently non-sustained** — 4-5 of the first 5 years were "Non-sustained WF"

<br>

## Demographic variables

Turning to the non-sustained-only decomposition (`non_sustained.cat`), the demographic associations tell a genuinely different story than the combined `disconnected.cat` measure did — several variables that were weak or negligible for overall disconnection reappear here with more signal, and the shape of the race/ethnicity finding changes entirely. This is exactly the kind of divergence the earlier driver decomposition (no-record-driven vs. non-sustained-driven vs. mixed) anticipated, and it's worth reading these results directly against that decomposition rather than in isolation.

**Economic status** shows the strongest association of any demographic variable examined here (Cramer's V = 0.086, p \< .001) — a striking reversal from the combined disconnection measure, where economic status was the *weakest* of the six demographic variables (V = 0.047) with only a negligible gap. Here, economically disadvantaged individuals show a meaningfully higher rate of persistent non-sustained employment (14.9%) than non-disadvantaged individuals (11.2%), and a correspondingly lower "never non-sustained" rate (32.1% vs. 39.6%). This confirms the suspicion raised by the earlier driver decomposition: economic status's relationship to disconnection isn't absent, it was being masked in the combined measure because economic disadvantage relates specifically to job *instability*, not to disappearing from Minnesota's employment records — separating the two reveals a real, substantive economic-status effect that the combined table obscured entirely.

**Special education status** shows the second-strongest association (Cramer's V = 0.076, p \< .001), essentially matching its strength in the combined measure (V = 0.075). Individuals with special education status show a notably higher persistent non-sustained rate (16.9%) than those without (11.8%), and a lower never-non-sustained rate (31.8% vs. 37.0%). Unlike economic status, this association was already visible in the combined table — special education status appears to be a genuine non-sustained-employment risk factor specifically, consistent across both measures.

**Gender** remains significant but is weaker here than in the combined measure (Cramer's V = 0.072 vs. 0.109 for `disconnected.cat`). Women still show a higher persistent non-sustained rate than men (15.2% vs. 11.6%), in the same direction as before, but a meaningful share of the gender gap found in the combined disconnection measure appears to run through no-record status rather than job instability specifically.

**English learner status and non-English home language** both show weaker, and notably **more polarized**, patterns than in the combined measure (English learner: V = 0.046; non-English home: V = 0.051). Rather than a simple "worse across the board" pattern, both groups show *higher* rates at both extremes: English learners have a higher never-non-sustained rate (38.1% vs. 35.4%) **and** a higher persistently non-sustained rate (16.1% vs. 12.6%), with correspondingly lower rates in the two middle (intermittent/broad) categories. Non-English-home individuals show an even starker version of this: a considerably higher never-non-sustained rate (41.8% vs. 34.9%) alongside a roughly *equal* persistently non-sustained rate (12.9% vs. 13.1%, essentially no gap). This is a genuinely different shape from the combined disconnection table, where non-English-home individuals showed a clearly and substantially elevated persistent disconnection rate (75.9% vs. 57.5%, per the earlier demographic summary) — that gap appears to be driven almost entirely by no-record status rather than job instability, since the non-sustained-only picture shows these groups splitting toward both stability and chronic instability rather than uniformly toward the negative outcome.

**Race/ethnicity** shows the weakest association among this group (Cramer's V = 0.040, p \< .001), but the composition of *which* groups are most at risk changes substantially from the combined table. Here, **Black graduates show by far the highest rate of persistent non-sustained employment (21.5%)** — well above Hispanic (15.0%), American Indian (17.0%), Asian/PI (12.9%), and White (12.5%) graduates. This is a meaningfully different picture from the combined disconnection measure, where American Indian graduates showed the highest overall persistent disconnection rate (70.6%) by a wide margin. Read together with the earlier decomposition finding that no-record status is the dominant driver of persistent disconnection overall, this suggests American Indian graduates' elevated combined disconnection rate runs disproportionately through no-record status, while Black graduates' risk is concentrated specifically in non-sustained (unstable, but present) employment — a substantively important distinction that points toward different underlying dynamics for the two groups and, potentially, different intervention approaches.

[**Summary of demographic variables for non-sustained-only disconnection**]{.underline}

Isolating non-sustained employment from the combined disconnection measure reshapes the demographic story considerably, and confirms that the driver decomposition matters for interpretation, not just for description. Economic status, nearly invisible in the combined measure, re-emerges as the strongest demographic predictor of non-sustained-specific risk — exactly the kind of masking effect the driver decomposition would predict, since economic disadvantage's relationship to disconnection appears to run through job instability rather than absence from the workforce record. Special education status and gender both remain significant in the same direction as before, though gender's effect roughly softens once no-record cases are removed. English learner status and non-English home language show a more polarized, bimodal pattern here than the uniformly worse pattern seen in the combined table, suggesting their strong combined-disconnection association is substantially a no-record story rather than a job-instability story. Most notably, the race/ethnicity picture inverts: Black graduates, not American Indian graduates, show the greatest vulnerability to persistent non-sustained employment specifically, while American Indian graduates' dominant role in the combined measure likely reflects their disproportionate representation in no-record status instead. This reinforces the earlier recommendation to treat the driver categories as analytically distinct going forward — the same demographic variable can look weak, moderate, or strong (and point to entirely different at-risk groups) depending on which component of disconnection is being examined, and any policy narrative built on the combined measure alone risks misattributing which groups need which kind of intervention.

## High school characteristics

Turning to high school characteristics for the non-sustained-only decomposition, the pattern diverges from the combined disconnection measure in several substantively important ways — most strikingly, the EDR finding **reverses direction entirely**, which is a significant addition to the picture built up so far.

**Local unemployment rate** is significant overall (F = 7.435, p \< .001), and shows a similar non-monotonic shape to the combined measure, though the specific comparisons that reach significance differ. **Intermittently non-sustained (+0.097, p = .001) and broadly non-sustained (+0.146, p \< .001) individuals come from areas with significantly higher local unemployment than those who are never non-sustained.** Persistently non-sustained individuals, however, are **not** significantly different from the never-non-sustained group (+0.076, p = .147), and none of the pairwise comparisons among intermittent, broad, and persistent reach significance. As with the combined measure, this suggests local unemployment context distinguishes *some* non-sustained experience from none at all, but doesn't clearly separate the persistently non-sustained from anyone else — the effect size remains small in practical terms (sumsq of 36.3 against 21,450.4 residual, well under 1% of variance explained).

**Local average wages show no relationship whatsoever** with non-sustained persistence (F = 0.073, p = .975) — an even more definitively null result than the already-null finding for the combined disconnection measure. Local wage competitiveness appears entirely unrelated to job-instability patterns specifically, reinforcing that whatever role local wages play elsewhere in this project (strong predictor of workforce attachment and, in the Part 2 region-only non-completer models, of regional retention specifically), it has no bearing on the *non-sustained* component of disconnection.

**Community type (`Dem_Desc`)** is weakly significant (Cramer's V = 0.035, p \< .001), similar in magnitude to the combined measure, but the pattern **reverses direction**. In the combined disconnection table, entirely rural graduates showed the *highest* persistent disconnection rate (54.5%). Here, entirely rural graduates show the **lowest** persistent non-sustained rate (10.7%) and the highest never-non-sustained rate (39.2%), while town/rural mix graduates show the **highest** persistent non-sustained rate (13.6%). This is a genuinely important divergence worth flagging explicitly: entirely rural graduates' apparent disadvantage in the combined measure does not carry over to job instability specifically — if anything, they show the most stable non-sustained profile of the three community types. Whatever drives entirely rural graduates' elevated combined disconnection rate is more likely concentrated in no-record status than in cycling through unstable work.

**EDR** is weakly significant (Cramer's V = 0.044, p \< .001) and shows the **most striking reversal in this entire bivariate phase**. In the combined disconnection measure, EDR 8 showed the *highest* persistent disconnection rate (53.5%) of the three regions, while EDR 6E showed the *lowest* (45.8%). Here, for non-sustained employment specifically, **EDR 8 shows the *lowest* persistent non-sustained rate (11.6%) and the highest never-non-sustained rate (38.8%)**, while EDR 6E and EDR 6W are both modestly elevated and nearly identical to each other (14.2% and 14.1% persistently non-sustained, respectively). In other words, EDR 8's poor showing in the combined measure is **not** explained by job instability — EDR 8 graduates who work, work relatively steadily. This strongly suggests EDR 8's elevated combined persistent-disconnection rate is driven specifically by no-record status rather than non-sustained employment, a hypothesis directly testable once the no-record-specific table for EDR is available, and one that would be an important, genuinely new addition to the EDR story built up across this entire project.

[**Summary of high school characteristics for non-sustained-only disconnection**]{.underline}

The high school characteristics block reinforces, more clearly than any other block examined so far, why decomposing the combined disconnection measure matters. Local unemployment retains a similar (non-monotonic, weak) shape to the combined measure, and local wages remain entirely unrelated to disconnection in either specification. But community type and — especially — EDR both **reverse direction** between the combined and non-sustained-specific measures. Entirely rural graduates and EDR 8 graduates both looked disadvantaged in the combined table but show the *most* stable non-sustained employment profiles here, meaning their combined-measure disadvantage is very likely concentrated in no-record status rather than job instability. This is the clearest evidence yet that the earlier decision to separate non-sustained from no-record disconnection was the right call: at least two variables in this block would have been fundamentally mischaracterized — as risk factors for job instability — had the analysis stopped at the combined measure. The no-record-specific tables, once available, should be examined closely for exactly the EDR 8 and entirely-rural patterns hypothesized here.

## High school academics

Turning to high school academic accomplishments for the non-sustained-only decomposition, this block produces the most striking reversal yet in this bivariate analysis — several of the strongest findings from the combined disconnection measure (CTE achievement, CTE course intensity, ACT composite score) either weaken substantially, lose significance, or reverse pattern entirely when isolated to non-sustained employment specifically, while one previously null finding (MCA Science) newly emerges as significant.

**CTE achievement level** remains significant but is considerably weaker here (Cramer's V = 0.052) than in the combined measure (0.106), and the pattern itself changes shape. In the combined table, CTE engagement was cleanly protective at every level. Here, individuals with no CTE participation show the **highest** never-non-sustained rate (41.7%, vs. 34.4% for Concentrators/Completors and 33.6% for Participants), while CTE Concentrators/Completors and Participants show **higher** intermittently non-sustained rates (40.6% and 38.9%, vs. 33.7% for No CTE) — and persistently non-sustained rates that are nearly identical across all three groups (12.6%, 13.9%, and 13.0%, respectively). In other words, CTE's dramatic protective effect on overall disconnection does **not** carry over to job stability specifically — CTE participants and non-participants end up persistently non-sustained at essentially the same rate. This strongly suggests CTE's powerful combined-measure protective effect operates primarily through keeping graduates *present in Minnesota's employment records at all* (avoiding no-record status), rather than through job stability once employed.

**Total CTE courses taken** shows the same reversal in even starker terms. The effect size collapses to roughly a seventh of its size in the combined measure (F = 16.582 here vs. F = 114.407 for `disconnected.cat`), and the clean monotonic dose-response found in the combined table disappears entirely. Instead, the pattern is **non-monotonic**: intermittently non-sustained individuals took significantly *more* CTE courses than the never-non-sustained group (+0.550, p \< .001) — the opposite direction from the combined measure — while persistently non-sustained (−0.330 vs. intermittent, p = .012) and broadly non-sustained (−0.285 vs. intermittent, p = .046) individuals took significantly fewer courses than the intermittently non-sustained group, but were **not** significantly different from the never-non-sustained group. This is the single clearest confirmation in this entire bivariate phase that CTE's protective role, as measured against the combined disconnection outcome, is not really a story about job-instability avoidance — it's a story about staying connected to Minnesota's workforce records at all.

**ACT composite score** loses significance entirely (F = 0.757, p = .518), a complete reversal from the combined measure's significant, counterintuitive "higher score, more disconnection" finding (F = 12.637, p \< .001). The achievement-versus-attachment tension identified in the combined table appears to run entirely through no-record status rather than job instability — among ACT-takers, score has no bearing on whether their employment, when present, is sustained or not.

**Having taken the ACT** remains significant but weaker (Cramer's V = 0.055 vs. 0.075 combined), and shows an unusual pattern worth noting alongside the CTE finding above: ACT-takers show a *lower* never-non-sustained rate (33.5% vs. 37.4% for non-takers) and a *higher* intermittently non-sustained rate (41.7% vs. 36.4%), while persistently non-sustained rates are close and modestly lower for takers (12.7% vs. 13.3%). As with CTE, this suggests ACT-taking's protective role in the combined measure is disproportionately about avoiding no-record status rather than avoiding job instability specifically — though a modest genuine protective signal against *persistent* non-sustained status does remain.

**PSEO participation loses significance** entirely (Cramer's V = 0.021, p = .249), down from an already-weak significant finding in the combined measure (p = .005). PSEO's minimal combined-measure protective effect does not survive decomposition.

**AP exam participation remains non-significant** (Cramer's V = 0.014, p = .429), consistent with its null finding in the combined measure.

**MCA Math** remains significant and retains essentially the same protective, largely monotonic pattern found in the combined measure (F = 14.384, p \< .001): persistently non-sustained individuals score significantly lower than both never-non-sustained (−0.173, p \< .001) and intermittently non-sustained individuals (−0.123, p \< .001), and broadly non-sustained individuals score significantly lower than never (−0.156, p \< .001) and intermittently non-sustained (−0.106, p = .003) as well. This is one of the few high-school-accomplishment measures whose relationship to disconnection is essentially unchanged by the non-sustained/no-record decomposition — MCA Math's protective association appears to be a genuine job-stability story, not primarily a records-presence story.

**MCA Reading** is significant and, notably, **stronger and cleaner here** than in the combined measure (F = 8.059, p \< .001 here vs. F = 5.524, p = .001 combined, where only one comparison reached significance). Here, persistently non-sustained individuals score significantly lower than both never-non-sustained (−0.131, p \< .001) and intermittently non-sustained individuals (−0.131, p \< .001). This is a case where decomposition *sharpens* a previously partial finding rather than weakening it.

**MCA Science, non-significant in the combined measure (p = .115), newly emerges as significant here** (F = 9.900, p \< .001) — a genuinely new finding not visible in the combined table. Persistently non-sustained individuals score significantly lower than never-non-sustained (−0.157, p \< .001), intermittently non-sustained (−0.128, p \< .001), and broadly non-sustained individuals (−0.096, p = .033). This is worth flagging explicitly: MCA Science appeared to have no relationship with disconnection at all until the non-sustained component was isolated, at which point a real, monotonic, protective association appeared.

[**Summary of high school academic accomplishments for non-sustained-only disconnection**]{.underline}

This block delivers the clearest evidence yet that the earlier decision to separate non-sustained employment from no-record status was analytically essential, not just descriptively tidy. The two strongest findings from the combined disconnection measure — CTE achievement and CTE course intensity — both weaken dramatically and change shape once no-record cases are removed, revealing that CTE's headline protective effect operates mainly by keeping graduates present in Minnesota's wage records, not by making their employment more stable once they're in it. ACT composite score's counterintuitive achievement-risk finding disappears entirely under the same decomposition. Meanwhile, the three MCA subject scores tell the opposite story: MCA Math holds essentially steady, MCA Reading strengthens, and MCA Science — null in the combined measure — emerges as a genuine, monotonic predictor here. Taken together, this suggests two categorically different mechanisms are at work: CTE and ACT-taking primarily prevent graduates from disappearing from the employment record altogether, while the MCA subject scores (especially Math and, now, Science) are more specifically tied to whether the employment someone does have is stable. This distinction should be central to the eventual synthesis and to any policy framing — a CTE-expansion strategy and an academic-preparation strategy are likely to be effective against two different components of disconnection, not interchangeable levers against the same problem.

## Post-secondary

Turning to postsecondary attendance without completion (`attended.ps`) for the non-sustained-only decomposition, this variable remains significant and shows a genuine, substantial protective effect (Cramer's V = 0.087, p \< .001) — though it is notably weaker here than in the combined disconnection measure (0.132), consistent with the pattern seen throughout this decomposition where combined-measure effects concentrated partly in no-record status.

**Having attended some postsecondary education is meaningfully protective against persistent non-sustained employment.** Attendees show a persistently non-sustained rate of 9.9%, compared to 14.9% for those who never attended — a 5-percentage-point gap. This protective pattern extends through the broadly non-sustained category as well (11.1% vs. 13.5%), and attendees also show a notably higher intermittently non-sustained rate (42.1% vs. 36.5%), with never-non-sustained rates similar between groups (36.9% vs. 35.1%).

**This effect is genuinely present here, unlike several of the high-school-accomplishment variables examined in the prior block, but it is meaningfully smaller than its combined-measure counterpart.** In the combined table, the persistent-disconnection gap between attendees and non-attendees was 12.1 percentage points (42.8% vs. 54.9%); here, isolated to non-sustained employment, the gap is less than half that size (5.0 points). This suggests — consistent with the pattern established throughout this entire non-sustained-only decomposition — that `attended.ps`'s strong combined-measure protective effect is partly, though not entirely, a story about staying present in Minnesota's employment records rather than about job stability specifically. Unlike CTE achievement and CTE course intensity, which lost nearly all of their combined-measure signal once isolated to non-sustained employment, `attended.ps` retains a real, substantial, and still second-strongest-in-this-block protective association even after decomposition — suggesting some of its benefit genuinely operates through job stability, not just records presence.

[**Summary**]{.underline}

`attended.ps` remains one of the stronger and more robust protective factors identified across both the combined and non-sustained-specific disconnection measures, distinguishing it from CTE achievement and CTE course intensity, whose combined-measure protective effects turned out to be driven almost entirely by no-record avoidance rather than job stability. This reinforces attempting postsecondary education, even without completing it, as a genuinely dual-purpose protective factor — helping graduates both stay present in Minnesota's workforce records and, to a real if smaller degree, avoid unstable employment specifically — making it, alongside MCA Math and MCA Reading, one of the few variables in this analysis whose protective role survives the non-sustained/no-record decomposition largely intact.

## Summary: Bivariate Predictors of Non-Sustained Employment Persistence (`non_sustained.cat`)

| Rank | Variable | Block | Statistic | Significant? |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | Total CTE courses taken | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 13,173) = 16.582, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 2 | MCA Math | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 11,869) = 14.384, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 3 | MCA Science | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 9,147) = 9.900, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 4 | MCA Reading | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 11,698) = 8.059, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 5 | Average county unemployment rate | HS Characteristics | F(3, 13,173) = 7.435, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 6 | Attended postsecondary (attended.ps) | Postsecondary | Cramér's V = 0.087, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 7 | Economic status | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.086, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 8 | Special education status | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.076, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 9 | Gender | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.072, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 10 | ACT participation (took.ACT) | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.055, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 11 | CTE achievement status | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.052, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 12 | Non-English home language | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.051, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 13 | English learner status | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.046, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 14 | Economic Development Region (EDR) | HS Characteristics | Cramér's V = 0.044, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 15 | Race/Ethnicity | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.040, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 16 | District rurality (Dem_Desc) | HS Characteristics | Cramér's V = 0.035, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 17 | PSEO participation | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.021, p = .249 | **No** |
| 18 | ACT composite score | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 5,482) = 0.757, p = .518 | **No** |
| 19 | AP exam participation | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.014, p = .429 | **No** |
| 20 | Average county wages (% of state avg.) | HS Characteristics | F(3, 13,173) = 0.073, p = .975 | **No** |

Across all four blocks, most variables remain statistically significant when disconnection is isolated to non-sustained employment specifically, but effect sizes are, without exception, weaker than their counterparts in the combined `disconnected.cat` measure — several dramatically so. More importantly, the *composition and direction* of what predicts non-sustained-specific risk differs substantially from what predicts combined disconnection, confirming that the decision to separate non-sustained employment from no-record status earlier in this analysis was not just a descriptive refinement but a genuine analytical necessity.

**High school accomplishments contain both the strongest findings in this table and the clearest evidence of mechanism divergence from the combined measure.** Total CTE courses taken remains the top-ranked variable, but its effect size collapses to roughly a seventh of its combined-measure magnitude (F = 16.58 here vs. 114.41 for `disconnected.cat`), and the clean monotonic dose-response found in the combined table disappears — replaced by a non-monotonic pattern where intermittently non-sustained individuals actually took the *most* CTE coursework. CTE achievement status shows the same reversal in miniature: individuals with no CTE participation show the highest never-non-sustained rate, and persistently non-sustained rates are nearly identical across all three CTE achievement levels. ACT composite score, significant and counterintuitively risk-associated in the combined measure, loses significance entirely here (p = .518). Together, these findings indicate that CTE's and ACT score's strong combined-measure associations operate substantially — in ACT score's case, seemingly entirely — through keeping graduates present in Minnesota's employment records, not through making their employment more stable once present. By contrast, the three MCA subject scores tell a different story: MCA Math holds essentially steady in both magnitude and direction, MCA Reading strengthens and cleans up relative to the combined measure, and MCA Science — non-significant in the combined table — emerges here as a genuine, monotonic predictor. This split suggests two distinct mechanisms are at work in this block: CTE and ACT-taking primarily prevent disappearance from the workforce record, while the MCA subject scores (Math and, newly, Science) are more specifically tied to employment stability itself.

**High school characteristics show a similarly weak but genuinely reshuffled pattern.** Average county unemployment rate retains roughly the same non-monotonic shape found in the combined measure — elevated for intermittent and broad non-sustained employment, but not clearly distinguishing the persistently non-sustained from the never-non-sustained. Average county wages remains entirely unrelated to disconnection in either specification. District rurality and EDR both show the most striking reversals in this entire table: entirely rural graduates and EDR 8 graduates, both of whom appeared disadvantaged in the combined measure, show the *most stable* non-sustained employment profiles here — meaning their combined-measure disadvantage almost certainly runs through no-record status rather than job instability.

**Demographic characteristics show a materially different picture than the combined measure, both in strength and in which groups are most at risk.** Economic status re-emerges as one of the strongest predictors in this table (rank 7 of 20, and the strongest demographic variable), a striking change from its near-null role in the combined measure — this appears to be a genuine masking effect resolved by the decomposition. Special education status and gender both remain significant in familiar directions, though gender's effect softens somewhat relative to the combined table. English learner status and non-English home language show more polarized, bimodal patterns here (elevated at both the "never" and "persistent" extremes) rather than the uniformly worse pattern seen in the combined measure, suggesting their combined-measure association runs disproportionately through no-record status. Race/ethnicity shows the most substantively important shift: Black graduates, not American Indian graduates, show the highest rate of persistent non-sustained employment here — the opposite of the combined table's finding, where American Indian graduates showed by far the highest overall persistent disconnection rate. This points toward genuinely different risk profiles for these two groups: American Indian graduates' disconnection appears concentrated in absence from the record, while Black graduates' disconnection appears concentrated in job instability specifically.

**Attended postsecondary education without completion (`attended.ps`) is the one variable in this analysis that retains a substantial, largely intact protective effect across both the combined and non-sustained-specific measures**, distinguishing it clearly from CTE, whose protective role turned out to be driven almost entirely by records-presence rather than job stability. While its effect size is meaningfully smaller here than in the combined table (a 5.0-percentage-point persistent-rate gap vs. 12.1 points combined), it remains one of the strongest and most robust findings in this table, suggesting `attended.ps` genuinely operates through both channels — helping graduates stay present in the workforce record *and*, to a real degree, helping stabilize the employment they do have.

**Overall Conclusion**

Decomposing overall disconnection into its non-sustained-employment component fundamentally changes which variables matter, how strongly, and in some cases which direction they run — confirming that "persistent disconnection" was never a single phenomenon and that this earlier analytical decision was essential rather than optional. The strongest predictors of the combined measure (CTE achievement, CTE course intensity, ACT score) turn out to be primarily — in ACT score's case, apparently entirely — predictors of whether a graduate disappears from Minnesota's employment record, not of whether their employment is stable when present. Meanwhile, economic status, MCA Science, and the Black/American Indian race-ethnicity split all reveal genuine, substantive associations with job instability specifically that were invisible or misattributed in the combined table. The clearest, most durable protective factors against non-sustained employment specifically — as opposed to disconnection broadly — are `attended.ps`, MCA Math, and MCA Reading, none of which lost meaningful ground in this decomposition. For the policy narrative, this means CTE expansion remains a strong lever for keeping graduates connected to Minnesota's workforce at all, but a genuinely different set of levers — attempted postsecondary education, and academic preparation as measured by MCA rather than ACT — appears more directly tied to whether the work graduates do find is stable once they have it. The next natural step, and the one that would resolve the remaining ambiguity in nearly every finding above, is running this same bivariate sequence against the no-record-specific persistence measure, since that table would confirm directly whether the variables that lost signal here (CTE, ACT score, EDR, Dem_Desc) show the mirror-image strong effects there that this analysis predicts.

<br>

# Relationship Between Individual Characteristics and having No Minnesota Employment Categories

The next sections focus on exploring what relationships exist between individual characteristics and the frequency of having no Minnesota employment record in the first 5 years after formal education.

- **Never no-record** — 0 of the first 5 years (post-high-school or post-postsecondary-exit) had no Minnesota employment record
- **Intermittently no-record** — 1-2 of the first 5 years had no Minnesota employment record
- **Broadly no-record** — exactly 3 of the first 5 years had no Minnesota employment record
- **Persistently no-record** — 4-5 of the first 5 years had no Minnesota employment record

<br>

## Demographic variables

Turning to the no-MN-employment-record decomposition (`no_record.cat`), this table provides the direct test of several hypotheses raised throughout the non-sustained-only analysis — and confirms the central one in striking fashion: American Indian graduates' dominant role in the combined disconnection measure is, in fact, driven overwhelmingly by no-record status rather than job instability, while Black graduates show the opposite pattern.

**Non-English home language** shows the strongest demographic association with no-record persistence (Cramer's V = 0.086, p \< .001) — larger than its role in either the combined measure (0.066) or the non-sustained-only measure (0.051), and the largest raw gap of any variable in this table. Individuals from non-English-speaking homes show a persistently no-record rate of 33.6%, compared to 22.8% for those from English-speaking homes — an 10.8-percentage-point gap — and a correspondingly lower never-no-record rate (43.7% vs. 52.8%). This is the clearest evidence yet that non-English home language's substantial combined-measure association (75.9% vs. 57.5% persistent disconnection, per the earlier demographic summary) runs disproportionately through absence from Minnesota's wage records rather than through cycling in and out of unstable jobs — consistent with, and now confirming, the pattern already suspected from the non-sustained table's more muted, bimodal version of this same relationship.

**Race/ethnicity** shows the single most important confirming finding in this entire decomposition. **American Indian graduates show the highest persistent no-record rate of any group (32.8%)**, closely followed by Asian/PI graduates (31.2%), while **Black graduates show the *lowest* persistent no-record rate of any group (20.5%)** — below Hispanic (28.9%) and White (23.1%) graduates as well. This is a direct, clean confirmation of the hypothesis raised after the EDR and Dem_Desc reversals in the earlier high-school-characteristics table: American Indian graduates' overwhelming dominance in the combined disconnection measure (70.6% persistent disconnection, by far the highest of any group) is now shown to run specifically through no-record status, not job instability, where American Indian graduates were not the most at-risk group. Black graduates show precisely the mirror-image pattern: elevated risk in the non-sustained-only table (21.5%, the highest of any racial/ethnic group there) paired with the *lowest* no-record risk here. Together, these two tables now fully explain the combined-measure race/ethnicity story: American Indian disconnection is a records-absence phenomenon; Black disconnection is a job-instability phenomenon. These are genuinely different problems requiring genuinely different interventions, and this distinction should be a headline finding in the eventual synthesis.

**English learner status** remains significant (Cramer's V = 0.053, p \< .001), similar in magnitude to its non-sustained-only association (0.046) and somewhat weaker than the combined measure (0.067). English learners show a persistently no-record rate of 29.9%, compared to 23.3% for non-English-learners — a real, if more moderate, gap that splits roughly evenly between the two component measures rather than concentrating heavily in either one.

**Economic status** shows a significant association (Cramer's V = 0.059, p \< .001), but here — notably — **it runs in the opposite direction from the non-sustained-only table.** Economically disadvantaged individuals show a *lower* persistently no-record rate (22.2%) than non-disadvantaged individuals (26.1%), while their intermittently no-record rate is elevated (19.9% vs. 16.2%). This is a genuinely important reversal worth naming explicitly: economic disadvantage is a real risk factor for job *instability* specifically (per the non-sustained table, where disadvantaged individuals showed a *higher* persistent rate), but appears mildly *protective* against chronic absence from Minnesota's employment record altogether. A plausible explanation is that economically disadvantaged non-completers may be more tied to local, lower-wage work out of necessity, keeping them present in the wage record even when that work is unstable, whereas those with more economic flexibility may be like more likely to leave the labor force, the state, or the formal economy entirely for a period. This is worth flagging as a nuance for the write-up rather than collapsing economic status into a single "risk factor" narrative.

**Special education status** shows the **weakest association in this entire table** (Cramer's V = 0.037, p \< .001) and, critically, **shows almost no gap in the persistently no-record category at all** (24.5% for special education status vs. 24.0% for others — essentially identical). Combined with special education status's real, substantial association with the non-sustained-only measure (Cramer's V = 0.076, the second-strongest demographic finding there), this confirms that special education status's role in disconnection is overwhelmingly, perhaps almost entirely, a job-instability story — not a records-absence story. This is a clean, interpretable finding: special education completers who are disconnected are disconnected because their employment is unstable, not because they're missing from the workforce data.

**Gender** shows a comparatively weak association here (Cramer's V = 0.040, p \< .001) — the weakest of gender's three showings across the combined (0.109), non-sustained-only (0.072), and no-record (0.040) measures. Women still show a modestly higher persistently no-record rate (25.9% vs. 22.8%), but this progressive weakening across the three tables suggests gender's substantial combined-measure effect is disproportionately a non-sustained-employment story, with only a residual, smaller no-record component.

[**Summary of demographic variables for no-record-only disconnection**]{.underline}

This table resolves the central open question raised by the non-sustained-only decomposition: which demographic patterns in the combined disconnection measure were driven by job instability versus records absence. The clearest and most important resolution is race/ethnicity — American Indian graduates' severe combined-measure disadvantage is now shown to be a no-record phenomenon, while Black graduates' combined-measure risk is a non-sustained-employment phenomenon, a clean split that should anchor how these two groups' disconnection risk is discussed and addressed going forward. Non-English home language similarly concentrates its strongest signal here rather than in the non-sustained table, confirming that language-related disconnection risk is disproportionately about disappearing from the workforce record rather than cycling through unstable jobs. Special education status shows the mirror pattern — essentially all of its risk is job-instability-based, with almost none of it tied to no-record status. Economic status offers the most surprising and nuanced finding of the entire decomposition: it's a genuine risk factor for job instability but a mild protective factor against no-record status, a direction reversal that would have been completely invisible in the combined measure and deserves explicit, careful framing in the write-up rather than a single blanket "economic disadvantage increases disconnection risk" statement. Gender, by contrast, shows its strongest association in the non-sustained table and its weakest here, indicating its combined-measure effect is concentrated mostly, though not entirely, in job instability. Altogether, these three demographic tables (combined, non-sustained, no-record) now form a complete and mutually reinforcing picture: disconnection is not one problem with one set of risk factors, and nearly every demographic variable examined points toward a different primary mechanism once properly decomposed.

## High school characteristics

Turning to high school characteristics for the no-record decomposition, this table delivers direct, clean confirmation of the two hypotheses raised in the non-sustained-only analysis — both EDR and community type reverse exactly as predicted, and both reversals are stronger here than either weaker signal seen previously, confirming this is the table where their true story lives.

**EDR shows the strongest association of any high-school-characteristic variable across all three disconnection tables examined so far** (Cramer's V = 0.086, p \< .001) — stronger than its showing in either the combined measure (0.053) or the non-sustained-only measure (0.044). **EDR 8–Southwest shows by far the highest persistent no-record rate (28.0%) and the lowest never-no-record rate (46.5%) of the three regions**, while EDR 6E shows the lowest persistent no-record rate (20.4%) and the highest never-no-record rate (59.0%); EDR 6W sits in between (22.3% persistent, 49.7% never). This is a direct, clean confirmation of the hypothesis raised in the non-sustained-only writeup: EDR 8's poor showing in the combined disconnection measure is now shown to be driven specifically by no-record status, not job instability — where, per the earlier non-sustained table, EDR 8 graduates actually showed the *most* stable employment profile of the three regions. Read together, all three tables now tell a fully coherent EDR story: EDR 8 graduates who work, work steadily, but EDR 8 has the highest rate of graduates who simply disappear from Minnesota's wage records altogether, and that is what drives its disadvantage in the combined measure.

**Community type (`Dem_Desc`)** is also stronger here (Cramer's V = 0.056, p \< .001) than in either the combined (0.025) or non-sustained-only (0.035) measures, and confirms the second hypothesis raised previously. **Entirely rural graduates show the highest persistent no-record rate (30.1%)** — notably higher than town/rural mix (22.6%) and urban/town/rural mix (27.0%) — and the lowest never-no-record rate (43.5%). This directly confirms that entirely rural graduates' elevated combined-measure disconnection rate is a records-absence story, not a job-instability story, exactly as the non-sustained table's reversed pattern (entirely rural graduates showing the *most* stable non-sustained profile) predicted.

**Local unemployment rate** is significant (F = 20.031, p \< .001) and shows the clearest, most fully monotonic pattern of any continuous variable examined across all three disconnection tables: the never-no-record group comes from areas with the **highest** local unemployment, declining step-wise through intermittently no-record (−0.102 vs. never, p = .004), broadly no-record (−0.164 vs. never, p = .003), to persistently no-record (−0.202 vs. never, p \< .001; and significantly lower than intermittently no-record as well, −0.099, p = .021). In other words, **graduates from higher-unemployment areas are less likely to disappear from Minnesota's employment record, not more.** This is a genuinely important and counterintuitive finding worth connecting explicitly to the economic-status reversal found in the prior demographic table (where economic disadvantage was mildly *protective* against no-record status): a plausible unifying explanation is that graduates from higher-unemployment, more economically constrained areas may have fewer options to leave the local labor market or state entirely, keeping them present in Minnesota's wage data even when the work available to them is scarce or unstable — while graduates from lower-unemployment, more economically flexible areas have more latitude to leave the workforce, leave the state, or pursue unrecorded paths (e.g., further education elsewhere, informal work, military service) that would register as "no record" here.

**Local average wages show a real but very weak association** (F = 3.931, p = .008) — the only significant pairwise comparison is intermittently no-record vs. never no-record (+0.005, p = .005), with every other comparison non-significant. This is a much smaller and less consequential local-wage effect than found for local unemployment in this same table, and smaller than local wages' role in the workforce-attachment models examined earlier in this project.

[**Summary of high school characteristics for no-record-only disconnection**]{.underline}

This table closes the loop on both predictions carried forward from the non-sustained-only analysis: EDR 8 and entirely rural community type both show their strongest, clearest, and now-explained associations here, confirming that their combined-measure disadvantage is a no-record phenomenon rather than a job-instability one. Local unemployment rate produces the cleanest monotonic relationship found for any continuous variable across all three disconnection tables, and its counterintuitive direction (higher local unemployment, less likely to disappear from the record) offers a coherent explanation that dovetails with the economic-status reversal found in the demographic table — both point toward economically constrained circumstances functioning as a tether that keeps graduates connected to Minnesota's wage data even when broader workforce outcomes are poor. Local wages remain a comparatively minor factor throughout this entire no-record decomposition. Taken together with the demographic findings, the high-school-characteristics block confirms that this project's earlier EDR and community-type patterns — first flagged as puzzling reversals in the non-sustained-only table — have a clean, complete, and now fully evidenced explanation: they were never about job stability at all, they were about who stays in the data and who doesn't.

## High school academics

Turning to high school academic accomplishments for the no-record decomposition, this table delivers the final, decisive piece of evidence for the mechanism-splitting hypothesis built up across the entire bivariate analysis — CTE, ACT-taking, ACT score, and PSEO all show their strongest or newly-significant associations here, while the three MCA subject scores, protective in the non-sustained table, disappear almost entirely.

**Total CTE courses taken shows the single strongest continuous association found anywhere in this entire disconnection analysis** (F = 124.570, p \< .001; sumsq of 5,475.2, even larger than the combined measure's 5,039.9) — a fully monotonic decline, with persistently no-record individuals taking dramatically fewer courses than every other category (−1.58 courses vs. never no-record, p \< .001; −1.14 vs. intermittently no-record, p \< .001; −0.88 vs. broadly no-record, p \< .001). This is now clearly the true home of CTE course intensity's protective power: its effect here exceeds even its combined-measure showing, while its non-sustained-only effect (F = 16.58) was an order of magnitude smaller. **CTE achievement status** tells the identical story: the strongest categorical association found in this entire analysis (Cramer's V = 0.117, exceeding both the combined measure's 0.106 and the non-sustained table's 0.052). Persistent no-record status is 19.4% for CTE Concentrators/Completors, 22.3% for Participants, and 36.8% for those with no CTE participation — a 17.4-point gap, nearly matching the raw gap seen in the combined table. **This fully confirms the hypothesis raised in the accomplishments-block writeup for the non-sustained table: CTE's powerful protective effect operates almost entirely through keeping graduates present in Minnesota's employment records, not through stabilizing the work they do once employed.**

**Having taken the ACT** shows a stronger association here (Cramer's V = 0.081) than in the non-sustained table (0.055), close to its combined-measure strength (0.075). ACT-takers show a persistently no-record rate of 20.2%, compared to 26.9% for non-takers — a real, substantial gap, confirming ACT-taking's protective role is likewise concentrated disproportionately in records-presence rather than job stability.

**ACT composite score** is significant here (F = 16.512, p \< .001) — a reversal from its complete loss of significance in the non-sustained table (p = .518) — and, notably, runs in the **same counterintuitive risk direction found in the combined measure**: persistently no-record test-takers scored significantly higher, on average, than never-no-record test-takers (+1.019, p \< .001), and intermittently and broadly no-record test-takers also scored significantly higher than never-no-record test-takers (+0.580 and +0.632, both p \< .05). **This resolves the achievement-versus-disconnection puzzle raised earlier: the counterintuitive "higher ACT score predicts more disconnection" finding from the combined table is a no-record phenomenon, not a job-instability phenomenon** — among ACT-takers, higher scores specifically predict a greater likelihood of disappearing from Minnesota's wage records (plausibly reflecting higher-scoring students pursuing opportunities, education, or employment outside Minnesota), not a greater likelihood of unstable in-state employment.

**PSEO participation is significant here** (Cramer's V = 0.053, p \< .001) — its strongest showing across all three disconnection tables, a reversal from its loss of significance in the non-sustained table (p = .249). PSEO participants show a persistently no-record rate of 19.4%, compared to 25.4% for non-participants. This is a genuinely important finding worth flagging on its own: PSEO's minimal-looking combined-measure effect (the weakest significant finding in that table) turns out to mask a real, moderate protective association that is entirely concentrated in no-record status — consistent with PSEO's role elsewhere in this project as an early-college-credit pathway that likely keeps participants oriented toward continued engagement with Minnesota institutions and, by extension, its wage-record system.

**AP exam participation remains non-significant** (Cramer's V = 0.011, p = .654) — the third and final confirmation that AP exam participation has no measurable relationship with disconnection under any specification examined in this project.

**MCA Math loses significance entirely** (F = 0.865, p = .458) — a complete reversal from its significant, protective findings in both the combined measure (p \< .001) and, especially, the non-sustained table (p \< .001, its cleanest and strongest showing there). **MCA Reading likewise loses significance entirely** (F = 0.127, p = .944), reversing its significant finding in the non-sustained table. Together, these confirm the mirror-image hypothesis to the CTE finding above: **MCA Math and MCA Reading's protective associations are genuinely, specifically job-stability stories — they have essentially nothing to do with whether a graduate stays present in Minnesota's employment records.**

**MCA Science shows a weaker, murkier, and partially counterintuitive pattern** here (F = 3.885, p = .009) than in the clean, monotonic protective finding from the non-sustained table. The only significant pairwise comparison is broadly no-record vs. never no-record, and it runs in the **opposite** direction from a protective story (+0.108, p = .031 — broadly no-record individuals scored *higher* on MCA Science than never-no-record individuals). The persistently-no-record comparison is not significant (p = .086, though also trending positive). This inconsistency is worth flagging rather than smoothing over: MCA Science's relationship with disconnection appears genuinely different in shape from MCA Math and MCA Reading, and its earlier clean finding in the non-sustained table doesn't repeat itself here in a straightforward way.

[**Summary of high school academic accomplishments for no-record-only disconnection**]{.underline}

This final block completes the mechanism-splitting story that has run through this entire non-sustained/no-record decomposition, and does so with unusual clarity. CTE (both achievement level and course intensity), ACT-taking, ACT composite score, and PSEO participation all show their strongest, cleanest, or newly-significant associations specifically with no-record status — confirming that these variables' combined-measure protective (or, for ACT score, risk) effects are overwhelmingly about whether graduates remain present in Minnesota's employment records, not about whether their employment is stable once present. MCA Math and MCA Reading show the precise opposite pattern: significant and protective in the job-stability-specific non-sustained table, but entirely null here. This gives the full disconnection analysis a clean, two-track structure: **CTE engagement, ACT-taking, ACT achievement, and PSEO participation are records-presence levers; MCA Math and MCA Reading are job-stability levers**, with AP exam participation showing no relationship to either and MCA Science behaving inconsistently enough to warrant caution rather than a firm conclusion. This distinction should be central to the eventual synthesis: a workforce strategy aimed at keeping non-completers connected to Minnesota's labor market at all should prioritize CTE and ACT/PSEO engagement, while a strategy aimed at improving the *stability* of the work non-completers do find should look toward academic preparation as measured by MCA Math and Reading specifically — these are not interchangeable levers, and the combined disconnection measure alone would never have revealed which is which.

wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "ANOVA")
addWorksheet(wb, "TukeyHSD")
writeData(wb, "ANOVA", anova_df)
writeData(wb, "TukeyHSD", tukey_df)
saveWorkbook(wb, "Data/Claude/Non-college deeper/No record cat/High school accomplishments/MCA-M.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)

## Post-secondary

Turning to postsecondary attendance without completion (`attended.ps`) for the no-record decomposition, this variable remains significant and protective (Cramer's V = 0.070, p \< .001), though weaker here than in either the combined measure (0.132) or the non-sustained-only table (0.087) — the reverse pattern from most of the accomplishment variables examined in the prior block.

**Attending some postsecondary education without completing is protective against persistent no-record status.** Attendees show a persistently no-record rate of 20.7%, compared to 26.2% for those who never attended — a 5.5-percentage-point gap. Attendees also show a higher never-no-record rate (55.6% vs. 49.3%) and a modestly lower intermittently no-record rate (17.5% vs. 18.5%).

**This is the one variable in the entire accomplishments/postsecondary set where the effect is split roughly evenly between the two component measures rather than concentrated heavily in one.** The persistent-rate gap here (5.5 points) is nearly identical in size to the gap found in the non-sustained-only table (5.0 points), and both are meaningfully smaller than, but roughly proportional shares of, the combined-measure gap (12.1 points). Unlike CTE achievement, CTE course intensity, ACT-taking, ACT score, and PSEO — all of which showed their effects concentrated overwhelmingly in this no-record table — `attended.ps` appears to genuinely operate through both mechanisms simultaneously: it helps keep graduates present in Minnesota's employment records, and it modestly helps stabilize the employment they have. This dual-channel pattern is consistent with the earlier non-sustained-table finding that `attended.ps` was the one accomplishment-adjacent variable whose protective effect survived that decomposition largely intact.

[**Summary**]{.underline}

Across all three disconnection tables, `attended.ps` stands out as the most balanced protective factor identified in this analysis — meaningfully associated with both avoiding no-record status and avoiding non-sustained employment, rather than being a lever for one component and irrelevant to the other. This distinguishes it clearly from the sharply mechanism-specific variables found elsewhere: CTE, ACT-taking, ACT score, and PSEO participation are essentially records-presence levers, while MCA Math and MCA Reading are essentially job-stability levers. Having attempted postsecondary education, even without completing it, appears to be the one accomplishment in this entire analysis that meaningfully touches both halves of the disconnection problem at once.
