## Summary: Bivariate Predictors of No-Record Persistence (`no_record.cat`)

| Rank | Variable | Block | Statistic | Significant? |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | Total CTE courses taken | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 13,173) = 124.570, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 2 | CTE achievement status | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.117, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 3 | Average county unemployment rate | HS Characteristics | F(3, 13,173) = 20.031, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 4 | Economic Development Region (EDR) | HS Characteristics | Cramér's V = 0.086, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 5 | Non-English home language | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.086, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 6 | ACT participation (took.ACT) | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.081, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 7 | Attended postsecondary (attended.ps) | Postsecondary | Cramér's V = 0.070, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 8 | Economic status | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.059, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 9 | District rurality (Dem_Desc) | HS Characteristics | Cramér's V = 0.056, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 10 | English learner status | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.053, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 11 | PSEO participation | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.053, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 12 | ACT composite score | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 5,482) = 16.512, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 13 | Race/Ethnicity | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.046, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 14 | Gender | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.040, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 15 | Special education status | Demographics | Cramér's V = 0.037, p \< .001 | Yes |
| 16 | Average county wages (% of state avg.) | HS Characteristics | F(3, 13,173) = 3.931, p = .008 | Yes (weak) |
| 17 | MCA Science | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 9,147) = 3.885, p = .009 | Yes (mixed direction) |
| 18 | AP exam participation | HS Accomplishments | Cramér's V = 0.011, p = .654 | **No** |
| 19 | MCA Math | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 11,869) = 0.865, p = .458 | **No** |
| 20 | MCA Reading | HS Accomplishments | F(3, 11,698) = 0.127, p = .944 | **No** |

This is the third and final bivariate table in the disconnection decomposition, and it resolves nearly every open question raised by the combined and non-sustained-only analyses. Where those two tables raised hypotheses about which variables' effects were "really" about job instability versus records absence, this table provides the direct test — and confirms the predicted pattern with striking consistency across nearly every variable examined.

**High school accomplishments contain the two strongest findings in this entire disconnection analysis, and confirm that CTE's headline protective effect is fundamentally a records-presence story.** Total CTE courses taken shows the single largest continuous effect found anywhere across all three tables (F = 124.57, exceeding even its combined-measure showing), and CTE achievement status shows the strongest categorical effect found anywhere (Cramér's V = 0.117). Both dwarf their already-diminished showings in the non-sustained-only table (F = 16.58 and V = 0.052, respectively). ACT-taking, ACT composite score, and PSEO participation all follow the identical pattern — each stronger or newly significant here than in the non-sustained table, confirming that engagement-oriented accomplishments (CTE, ACT participation, PSEO) operate primarily by keeping graduates present in Minnesota's wage records, not by stabilizing the employment they find once there. ACT composite score's counterintuitive combined-measure finding (higher score, more disconnection) is also resolved here: it retains its risk-direction significance in this table, confirming that higher-scoring ACT-takers are specifically more likely to disappear from Minnesota's records — plausibly reflecting stronger students leaving the state — not more likely to hold unstable local jobs. By contrast, MCA Math and MCA Reading, both significant and protective in the non-sustained table, lose significance entirely here, confirming the mirror-image finding: their protective role is specifically about job stability and has nothing to do with records presence. MCA Science and AP exam participation round out the block with weak, inconsistent, or fully null results.

**High school characteristics show their strongest and most fully explained associations in this table.** EDR reaches its highest effect size across all three tables (Cramér's V = 0.086), with EDR 8 showing by far the highest persistent no-record rate and EDR 6E the lowest — directly confirming the hypothesis, raised after EDR's reversed pattern in the non-sustained table, that EDR 8's combined-measure disadvantage is a records-absence phenomenon rather than a job-instability one. District rurality shows the same confirming pattern: entirely rural graduates, who looked most stable in the non-sustained table, show the highest persistent no-record rate here. Local unemployment rate produces the cleanest, most fully monotonic relationship of any continuous variable in the entire analysis — counterintuitively, graduates from higher-unemployment areas are *less* likely to disappear from the record, plausibly because economic constraint limits their ability to leave the local labor market or state. Local wages remain a comparatively minor factor throughout.

**Demographic characteristics reveal the clearest and most consequential mechanism split in this entire project.** Non-English home language shows its strongest association here (Cramér's V = 0.086, exceeding its combined and non-sustained showings), confirming that language-related disconnection risk is disproportionately a records-absence story. Race/ethnicity delivers the single most important confirmation in the whole analysis: American Indian and Asian/PI graduates show the highest persistent no-record rates of any racial/ethnic group, while Black graduates show the *lowest* — the precise mirror image of the non-sustained table, where Black graduates showed the highest risk and American Indian graduates were comparatively unremarkable. This fully resolves the combined table's finding that American Indian graduates faced the most severe overall disconnection disadvantage in this project: that disadvantage is a records-absence phenomenon, while Black graduates' disconnection risk is a genuine job-instability phenomenon. Economic status shows a real but *reversed* direction relative to the non-sustained table: economic disadvantage is a risk factor for job instability but a mild *protective* factor against no-record status, most plausibly because economically constrained graduates have fewer options to leave the local labor market. Special education status, by contrast, shows almost no association here (the weakest finding in the table), confirming its role throughout this project as an almost purely job-instability-specific risk factor.

**Attended postsecondary education without completion (`attended.ps`) is the one variable whose protective effect is genuinely split across both mechanisms rather than concentrated in either.** Its persistent-rate gap here (5.5 points) closely matches its non-sustained-table gap (5.0 points), distinguishing it from every other accomplishment variable examined, all of which concentrated heavily in one mechanism or the other.

**Overall Conclusion**

Taken together, the three-table decomposition (combined, non-sustained, no-record) resolves what would otherwise have been a confusing or contradictory set of bivariate findings into a coherent, two-track structure. **CTE engagement, ACT participation and achievement, PSEO participation, EDR, district rurality, and non-English home language are, overwhelmingly, records-presence factors** — they determine whether a non-completer stays visible in Minnesota's wage data at all, and their effects were often understated or mischaracterized when only the combined measure was examined. **MCA Math, MCA Reading, and (in the opposite direction from expectation) economic status are job-stability-specific factors** — they shape whether a non-completer's employment, when present, is sustained, and several of their effects were nearly invisible in the combined table. Race/ethnicity cleanly splits by group rather than by mechanism: American Indian and Asian/PI graduates' disadvantage is a records-absence story, Black graduates' disadvantage is a job-instability story, and White and Hispanic graduates sit in between on both dimensions. Gender and special education status lean toward the job-instability side, while `attended.ps` is the sole variable operating meaningfully through both channels at once. This decomposition should fundamentally reshape how the eventual synthesis frames "persistent disconnection" for non-college graduates: it is not one problem with one set of causes and one obvious intervention, but at least two distinct problems — disappearing from Minnesota's workforce data, and cycling through unstable employment — that happen to share a combined label, respond to different levers, and disproportionately affect different demographic groups. Any policy recommendation drawn from this analysis should specify which of the two problems it is meant to address, since a strategy built around CTE expansion (a strong records-presence lever) would do little to address the job-instability risk driving Black graduates' and economically disadvantaged graduates' disconnection specifically, while a strategy built around academic preparation (MCA Math/Reading) would do little to address the records-absence risk driving American Indian, Asian/PI, and non-English-home graduates' disconnection.

<br>

# Full Synthesis: Workforce Disconnection Among Non-College Graduates in Southwest Minnesota

## **Purpose and Scope**

This phase of the analysis examined workforce participation trajectories among Southwest Minnesota high school graduates who did not complete a postsecondary credential (N = 13,177, 2011–2019 cohorts), using a five-year, persistence-based measure of "disconnection" rather than a single point-in-time outcome. Disconnection in a given year was defined as either non-sustained employment or no Minnesota employment record; individuals were classified across years 1–5 into four persistence categories (consistently attached, intermittently disconnected, broadly disconnected, persistently disconnected). Early in the analysis, this combined measure was decomposed into its two constituent parts — a non-sustained-employment persistence measure and a no-MN-record persistence measure — and each was tested against the same set of demographic, high-school-characteristic, and high-school-accomplishment variables used throughout this project, plus the single available postsecondary variable, `attended.ps`.

That decomposition turned out to be the defining methodological decision of this entire phase. What began as a routine breakdown became the mechanism for discovering that "persistent disconnection" is not one phenomenon but at least two, with different causes, different at-risk populations, and different policy implications.

## Key Findings

**Persistent disconnection is the modal, not exceptional, experience for non-college graduates — but the underlying descriptive picture is less severe than the headline figure suggests.** Half of this population (50.4%) is persistently disconnected across their first five years post-exit, while only 14.0% are consistently attached. But separating the two component measures immediately reframes this: persistent *non-sustained employment* alone describes only 13.1% of the population, while persistent *no-record status* alone describes 24.1% — meaning no-record status, not job instability, is the larger driver of the combined figure. A direct decomposition of the persistently disconnected group confirms this: 47.9% of persistently disconnected individuals are disconnected almost entirely because they're missing from Minnesota's wage records, compared to only 25.9% who are disconnected due to genuine job instability, with the remaining 26.2% alternating between both problems. The annual trajectory data reinforces this same divergence — combined sustained employment rises steadily from 32.1% to 42.0% over five years, but no-record status rises just as steadily, from 28.8% to 34.9%, and is the single largest category in every year.

**Every demographic, contextual, and academic variable examined told a substantively different — sometimes completely reversed — story depending on which component of disconnection was being measured, and the race/ethnicity finding is the clearest example.** In the combined measure, American Indian graduates showed by far the most severe disparity in this project (70.6% persistent disconnection, more than 20 points above White graduates). Decomposition revealed why: American Indian graduates' risk is concentrated almost entirely in no-record status (32.8% persistent no-record, the highest of any group), while their non-sustained-employment risk is unremarkable. Black graduates show the precise mirror image — the highest persistent non-sustained rate of any group (21.5%) but the *lowest* persistent no-record rate (20.5%). These are not variations on a single disadvantage; they are two different problems affecting two different groups, invisible as distinct phenomena until the measure was split.

**CTE engagement — the single strongest protective factor identified anywhere in this project's completer-focused work as well — turns out to operate almost entirely through keeping graduates present in Minnesota's employment records, not through stabilizing their employment once present.** CTE course intensity and CTE achievement level were the two strongest predictors in the combined measure. Decomposition showed both collapsed to a fraction of their effect size against non-sustained employment specifically (CTE achievement: Cramér's V falling from 0.106 to 0.052; CTE course intensity's clean monotonic dose-response disappearing into a non-monotonic pattern), while both *strengthened* against no-record status (CTE course intensity became the single largest continuous effect found anywhere in this analysis, F = 124.57; CTE achievement became the strongest categorical effect, V = 0.117). ACT-taking, ACT composite score, and PSEO participation followed the identical pattern — all concentrated their protective (or, for ACT score, risk) effects in the no-record measure.

**MCA Math and MCA Reading are the mirror image: genuine, specific predictors of job stability with no relationship to records presence at all.** Both were significant and protective in the combined measure and strengthened further when isolated to non-sustained employment, but both lost significance entirely against no-record status. This is the cleanest evidence in the entire analysis that academic achievement, as measured by the MCA, and academic achievement, as measured by the ACT, are doing genuinely different work here — ACT-taking and ACT score track records presence, while MCA scores track employment stability.

**Local unemployment rate and community type both reversed direction across the two component measures, revealing that entirely rural graduates and EDR 8 graduates are not actually at elevated risk of job instability — their combined-measure disadvantage is a records-absence story.** Entirely rural graduates and EDR 8 graduates both looked disadvantaged in the combined table, but showed the *most stable* non-sustained-employment profiles of any subgroup once decomposed — and then showed their most severe disadvantage specifically in the no-record table (EDR 8: highest persistent no-record rate of any region, 28.0%; entirely rural: highest persistent no-record rate of any community type, 30.1%). Local unemployment rate produced the cleanest and most counterintuitive finding of any continuous variable: graduates from higher-unemployment areas are consistently *less* likely to disappear from Minnesota's wage records, plausibly because economic constraint limits their ability to leave the local labor market or state — a pattern that dovetails with economic status's own reversal (a genuine risk factor for job instability, but a mild *protective* factor against no-record status).

**`attended.ps` is the one variable in this entire analysis that operates through both mechanisms roughly equally**, rather than concentrating its effect in one component or the other — distinguishing it from every high-school-accomplishment variable examined, all of which split sharply toward one mechanism or the other.

<br>

# The Story the Data Tells

The headline finding from this phase of the analysis — that half of Southwest Minnesota's non-college graduates are persistently disconnected from the workforce during their first five years out of school — turns out, on closer inspection, to describe two genuinely different problems wearing the same label.

The first problem is job instability: graduates who are working, but working unsteadily, cycling between meaningful and non-sustained employment year to year. This problem is real but comparatively contained — it describes roughly 13% of this population at its most persistent — and it has a fairly clean, coherent set of correlates: economic disadvantage, special education status, gender, and, most importantly, academic achievement as measured by MCA Math and Reading scores. It is, in short, the kind of disconnection a workforce-stability intervention is naturally built to address.

The second problem is disappearance: graduates who, for years at a stretch, simply have no detectable Minnesota employment record at all. This problem is larger — roughly 24% of the population at its most persistent, and the dominant driver of the combined 50.4% figure — and it has a completely different set of correlates: EDR (especially EDR 8), entirely rural community background, non-English home language, and, most strikingly, nearly every high-school engagement and achievement measure this project has treated as protective throughout its completer-focused work — CTE, ACT participation and score, and PSEO. Counterintuitively, local economic hardship is protective against this kind of disconnection rather than a risk factor, most plausibly because it removes the option of leaving. This is not primarily a story about unstable jobs; it is a story about who stays visible in Minnesota's economy at all, and who doesn't — whether because they left the state, left the formal labor market, pursued unrecorded paths, or something this data simply cannot see.

Race and ethnicity make the distinction unmistakable. American Indian graduates carry this project's most severe disparity, and that disparity is now shown to be almost entirely a disappearance story, not an instability story. Black graduates carry a disparity nearly as severe in the opposite direction — real job instability, but no elevated tendency to vanish from the record. A single "disconnection" narrative would have flattened these into one undifferentiated disadvantage; decomposed, they point toward two different populations needing two different kinds of attention.

The clearest practical implication is that CTE — this entire project's most consistently powerful lever for regional workforce attachment among both completers and non-completers — earns that reputation almost entirely by keeping graduates in the system, not by making the jobs they hold more stable. That is a genuinely valuable thing for a workforce strategy to accomplish, but it is not the same accomplishment as fixing job instability, and a strategy that leans on CTE expansion alone will do very little for the population — disproportionately Black, disproportionately economically disadvantaged, disproportionately special-education-status graduates — whose disconnection risk runs through unstable employment rather than absence from the record. That population's more promising lever, on this evidence, is closer to academic preparation as captured by the MCA than to career-technical engagement.

Taken as a whole, this phase of the analysis delivers a methodological lesson as important as its substantive findings: a combined outcome measure, however intuitively defined, can average together two mechanisms that pull in opposite directions and mask both in the process. Every major finding in this synthesis — the CTE/MCA split, the American Indian/Black race-ethnicity reversal, the EDR and rurality reversals, the economic-status reversal — was invisible in the combined table and only became legible once the measure was taken apart. Any recommendation that follows from this work should specify, explicitly, which of the two problems it is meant to solve — because on this evidence, they are not the same problem, and they do not share a solution.

write_csv(updated.master, "Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-non-college-grads-disconnection.csv")
